Prove it without revealing it

Act I

Prove a fact about a secret

~6 min · missions 1-4
1 The problem

Age checks are honeypots today

France mandates age verification for some sites; eIDAS 2.0 requires EU member states to offer identity wallets. The obvious build - upload a photo of your ID - creates exactly the centralised document store that keeps getting breached. The EU Digital Identity Wallet's answer is a zero-knowledge proof: your device convinces a site that "the holder is over 18" while revealing nothing else. You are about to run the conceptual core of that mechanism, then push well past it.

↩ From the talk · "What a ZK proof is" & "Terminology"Prover, proof, verifier - and the six-term breadcrumb (Claim → Public x → Witness w → Constraint → Circuit C → Statement). The two boxes below are exactly x and w, live.
Show the rules being proved (the circuit, in the Circom language) 

    
The key line is ok === 1: it makes "age ≥ minimum" a rule of the system, not a claim. If the rule does not hold, no valid proof exists. Act III is about what happens when a circuit forgets a line like this.

  






  
2 Missions 1-3 · Prove & verify

  
Generate the proof, then check it

  
Your browser computes a witness and builds a Groth16 proof over the BN254 curve - the same proof system securing billions on public chains. No server: you are the prover, and the verifier is this browser tab - on a blockchain it would be a smart contract.

  
↩ From the talk · "Proof systems" & "Interaction"Groth16 is the row you're running from that trade-off table. Verify is the non-interactive check from the Interaction slide - one message, no back-and-forth, checkable by anyone, any time after.

3 Mission 4 · Attack

  
Three ways to cheat - all rejected

  
A security claim you cannot attack is one you cannot trust. Predict, then attack.

  
↩ From the talk · "Security properties"Attack A tests completeness and soundness directly - the cards that say true statements always prove, and false ones can't. You're about to watch both hold, live rather than assumed.

  

    Prediction 2 - set your age to 15 above and generate. What happens?
    
    
    
    

  

  
Attack A - lie. Set age to 15 (min 18) above and click Generate. Watch the outcome, then set a truthful age and generate again so the next two attacks have a valid proof to work on.

  
Attack B - forge. Corrupt one byte of a valid proof, as an interceptor would.
    

  
Attack C - substitute the public input. Verify your valid proof against a different minimum than it was made for.
    






Act II
Prove membership without identity
~7 min · missions 5-7




  
4 A different shape of statement

  
"I belong to this set" - without revealing which member

  
Age was a range proof. The workhorse of real identity systems is a membership proof: prove your secret is one of the entries committed to in a public Merkle root, revealing nothing about which entry, or the others. The same primitive underlies two things you will hear about this week:

  

    
Selective disclosure (eIDAS)
Prove you hold a credential from some EU member state - enough to access a service - without disclosing your nationality.

    
Proof of innocence (Privacy Pools)
Prove your deposit is in the screened, approved set. You demonstrate membership of the clean set - not the absence of guilt, and not your identity.

  

  
↩ From the talk · "Two kinds of proof"This is the "proof of knowledge → privacy" row: hiding the witness (which member) is exactly what buys the privacy in both panels above - and in the Freedom Tool and shielded-transfer case studies.

  
Below is a 16-member approved set (think: 16 EU states). Pick which member you are - that choice is your secret - and prove membership. The verifier will only ever see the set's root.

6 Mission 7 · Swap with a neighbour

  
Anonymity set, made of humans

  
Export your membership proof and hand it to a neighbour. They verify it and learn you are a member of the set - not which member. You do the same with theirs. Two people, two proofs, one shared anonymity set, zero identities revealed.

  
↩ From the talk · "Security properties"Same zero-knowledge card as mission 3 - now tested by a sceptical human instead of the maths. Your neighbour holds the whole proof and still can't identify you.

  

    
A · Export your membership proof

      
      

    
B · Verify a neighbour's

      
      
      

  

  
Challenge while you hold their proof: work out which member your neighbour is. You have the complete artifact and the public member list. This impossibility - not the green tick - is the entire point.






Act III · CTF
Break it
~8 min · missions 8-9




  
7 Mission 8 · The challenge

  
A ZK proof is only as sound as its circuit

  
Everything so far assumed the circuit was written correctly. In the real world it often is not: under-constraint - a missing or loose constraint - is the single most common class of finding in ZK audits. Here is a circuit that is supposed to prove "age ≥ threshold" but has had its security removed. Read it, then defeat it.

  
↩ From the talk · "Tooling"This is the exact gap that slide named: "if the frontend omits a constraint, it proves the wrong statement - perfectly." You're about to be that missing constraint.

  

  

    
🚩 Goal: produce a proof that VERIFIES for the public statement "minimum = 18", while the true age is 15.

    
The only constraint left is age === threshold + diff. That is arithmetic in a finite field modulo a large prime p. Choose diff so the equation holds with age = 15 and threshold = 18. The panel below shows the field arithmetic live.

8 Mission 9 · The fix

  
One line restores soundness

  
The secure version adds exactly one thing: a range check forcing diff into [0, 2^8), so it cannot be a wrapped-around "negative". Send your winning exploit inputs to the fixed circuit and watch them fail.

  
↩ From the talk · "Security properties"Num2Bits(8) is the soundness card made concrete - the one-line difference between "no efficient cheating prover can succeed" and the exploit you just ran.

  
Show the one-line difference (secure circuit)

  
  






  
9 The honest fine print

  
Where the real fights are - and they're not all technical

  
Even a correctly written age circuit only proves you know a number ≥ 18, not that it's truly your age - production systems bind attributes to an issuer signature inside the circuit. And as mission 8 showed, correctness of the circuit is itself an open, human problem. A starter question per discipline:

  
↩ From the talk · "Trusted setup"The policy panel's ceremony question below is that slide's toxic-waste/MPC question, aimed at this exact circuit: today, one person - not a multi-party ceremony.

  

    
If you work in law
Your neighbour verified a proof about you in mission 7. Did they "process personal data" under the GDPR? Defend either answer.

    
If you work in HCI
Mission 8 showed a valid-looking proof of a false statement. How would you communicate "this system is sound" to a user who cannot audit a circuit?

    
If you work in policy
The keys here came from a ceremony run by one person. Who should run - and audit - the circuit and ceremony for 450 million EU citizens?

  

  
These same primitives compose into the EUDI Wallet's age-proof library, Swiss SWIYU selective disclosure, and the deployed privacy protocol we walk through next.
